Matthew 25:14-30. A master entrusts his property to three servants before departing. Two invest and double what they received. The third buries his talent in the ground: careful, cautious, preserving what was given.

When the master returns, the investors are celebrated. The burier is cast out.

His defense? “I knew you were a hard man. I was afraid.”

Fear produced paralysis. Paralysis produced nothing. Nothing earned judgment.

The Obvious Reading

The parable’s surface is clear enough: God expects return on investment. The waiting period isn’t passive: it’s the work window. The uncertainty of the master’s return timeline isn’t permission to freeze: it’s the condition under which faithful stewardship operates.

No one knew when he’d come back. Everyone was expected to build anyway.

The third servant’s sin wasn’t theft or waste. It was non-action. He preserved the capital perfectly and lost everything.

And we have spiritualized his failure into a virtue.

The Application We’re Avoiding

We’ve built an entire evangelical subculture around being the third servant: and calling it vigilance.

Watch prophecy conferences. Decode headlines against Revelation. Map current events to end-times charts. Consume content about the rapture, the tribulation, the antichrist, the mark. Stay alert. Stay ready. Any day now.

Meanwhile: Christian film is mostly bad. Christian music is mostly derivative. We’ve ceded the universities, abandoned the arts, forfeited law and medicine and architecture to whatever will fill the vacuum. We homeschool our own kids and let the empire’s schools catechize everyone else’s. We call this separation from the world.

The master returns and asks: “What did you build?”

“We watched a lot of YouTube videos about when you’d arrive.”

The Psyop

You know what that anxiety is doing to you. The algorithm feeds you dread because dread is engagement. Every geopolitical event becomes prophetic confirmation. Every cultural shift is birth pang. The church becomes a group of people staring at the sky while the city burns.

If you genuinely believed Jesus might return tomorrow, the rational response is to spend today building something that matters: because you want to be found working, not waiting. The irrational response is to stop planting vineyards because harvest might come early.

Jeremiah told the exiles in Babylon: 70 years. Build houses. Plant gardens. Seek the peace of the city where I’ve sent you. They thought they’d be home in two. God said think multigenerational.

The Actual Posture

Jesus could return tomorrow.

Build like He’s not coming for a thousand years.

Not as contradiction: as faithfulness. The servant commended isn’t the one who correctly predicted the return date. It’s the one who was working when the door opened.

Stop consuming end-times content. Seriously. Cold turkey. See what happens to your agency when you’re not microdosing apocalypse daily.

Start taking territory:

Make films non-Christians actually want to watch. Write novels that bear so much truth and beauty the world has to reckon with them. Build companies that set industry standards. Plant churches that don’t just survive but multiply. Start classical schools. Run for school board. Coach the local team. Create beauty that testifies to the God who invented beauty.

Not “Christian alternatives to secular things.” Just the best things: because excellence reflects divine character, and you can’t bring glory to God through mediocrity baptized with a worship song.

The Choice

Waiting or building. Escape or engagement. Bunker or beachhead.

The third servant’s logic sounds reasonable: the master is exacting, the stakes are high, better not risk it.

But preservation isn’t faithfulness. It’s fear calling itself wisdom.

The church that meets Jesus at His return should be running the best schools, making the best art, healing bodies and cities and cultures: not because we controlled the timeline but because we worked the timeline we were given.

The prophecy that matters isn’t which headline matches Revelation. It’s Habakkuk 2:14:

“The earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the Lord as the waters cover the sea.”

That’s not evacuation language. That’s saturation. Every domain, every discipline, every nation.

You can’t fill what you’ve abandoned.

Now build.
